sentences.text: Rimasuchus possessed a short and broad snout, a shape known as brevirostrine, which housed robust and blunt teeth unlike those of other crocodiles. These teeth were bicarinated, meaning they featured ridges on both the front and back surfaces to aid in gripping prey.
This large predator could grow to 7 meters or more in length, making it a formidable presence in its environment.
Fossil evidence suggests Rimasuchus preyed on large mammals, including primitive humans.

Predation by crocodiles, including Rimasuchus, is documented by tooth marks on Homo habilis fossils like OH 7, OH 8, and OH 35 at Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania. Bone damage on H. habilis remains includes bisected bite marks and perforations characteristic of crocodile predation.

The first fossil of Rimasuchus was collected by Lieutenant Colonel Arthur H. Lloyd in Wadi Moghara, Egypt, in the early 20th century. The holotype specimen CGM 15597 was described by Fourtau in 1918 as Crocodylus lloydi, a name that honors Arthur H. Lloyd, the discoverer of the fossils in Egypt.
The genus Rimasuchus was named by Storrs in 2003. The name Rimasuchus is derived from the Latin word rima, meaning 'crack', referencing the East African Rift Valley.

As a large semi-terrestrial predator, Rimasuchus likely competed directly with Nile crocodiles. Rimasuchus bones have been found in situ with other vertebrates including fish, birds, mammals like pigs, elephants, giraffes, bovines, rhinos, primates, and hominids such as Australopithecus afarensis.

Bone accumulations in beds I and II at the gorge have been specifically attributed to Rimasuchus. A trench containing primitive bovine bones, horses, specimen OH 7, and stone tools also contained Rimasuchus teeth.

Rimasuchus is now considered more closely related to modern African dwarf crocodiles (Osteolaemus) than to the genus Crocodylus. Rimasuchus is closely related to the modern dwarf crocodile Osteolaemus and belongs to the group Osteolaeminae. Rimasuchus belongs to the parent group Osteolaemini and is classified in the family Crocodylidae. Rimasuchus is a member of the class Reptilia.

Rimasuchus lived during the Early Miocene. Fossils of Rimasuchus date from approximately 1.88 to 7.44 million years ago. The genus Rimasuchus lived from the Burdigalian to the Late Pleistocene, between 20.45 and 0.0117 million years ago.

Rimasuchus fossils have been found in Egypt and possibly Libya. Rimasuchus fossils are found in sandstones and mudstones deposited in lakes and rivers. The earliest Rimasuchus specimens were found in North Africa, but how the species evolved and spread remains uncertain.

There has been very little study on ontogenetic variation in Rimasuchus and modern crocodiles. It is debated whether some Rimasuchus specimens are actually very large examples of Crocodylus niloticus due to similarities between them.
